topic: Amplifiers, oscillators and digital logic (G7B; 11 pool questions)

notes.front: What is self-oscillation in an RF amplifier?
notes.back: Unwanted oscillation an amplifier produces on its own, caused by internal feedback such as interelectrode capacitance.
notes.explanation: It turns an amplifier into an unintended oscillator, often making it unstable or generating spurious signals.
notes.example: An RF power amplifier that squeals or generates a signal even with no input applied is self-oscillating.

notes.front: What is neutralization?
notes.back: The process of counteracting the effects of interelectrode capacitance in an amplifier.
notes.explanation: It is done specifically to eliminate self-oscillation caused by that internal feedback path.
notes.example: A small neutralizing capacitor feeding an out-of-phase signal back to cancel unwanted internal feedback in a tube amplifier.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 8 glossary: "NEUTRALIZATION—The process of counteracting or \"neutralizing\" the effects of interelectrode capacitance."

notes.front: What is a Class A amplifier?
notes.back: An amplifier biased so the device conducts for the full input cycle, giving the least distortion but the lowest efficiency.
notes.explanation: Because the device never cuts off, the output waveform closely tracks the input, but a lot of power is wasted as heat.
notes.example: A Class A amplifier stage in a receiver's low-level audio chain, chosen for its clean, low-distortion output.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 7 glossary: "CLASS A AMPLIFIER OPERATION—The amplifier is biased so that variations in input signal polarities occur within the limits of cutoff and saturation."

notes.front: What is a Class B amplifier?
notes.back: An amplifier biased so the device's current is cut off for one half of the input signal.
notes.explanation: It sits between Class A's full conduction and Class C's shorter conduction, trading some distortion for better efficiency.
notes.example: A pair of Class B stages, each handling one half-cycle, combined to reproduce a full audio waveform.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 7 glossary: "CLASS B AMPLIFIER OPERATION—The amplifier is biased so that collector current is cut off for one-half of the input signal."

notes.front: What is a Class AB amplifier?
notes.back: An amplifier biased so the device's current is cut off for only a portion of the input signal, between Class A and Class B.
notes.explanation: It is a compromise that keeps distortion lower than Class B while improving efficiency over Class A.
notes.example: Many linear RF and audio power amplifiers run in Class AB to balance efficiency against distortion.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 7 glossary: "CLASS AB AMPLIFIER OPERATION—The amplifier is biased so that collector current is cut off for a portion of the alternation of the input signal."

notes.front: What is a Class C amplifier?
notes.back: An amplifier biased so current is cut off for more than one half of the input signal, giving the highest efficiency of the four classes.
notes.explanation: Its short conduction period saves power but badly distorts the waveform, so it suits constant-amplitude modes like FM rather than SSB.
notes.example: A Class C final amplifier stage used in an FM transmitter.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 7 glossary: "CLASS C AMPLIFIER OPERATION—The amplifier is biased so that collector current is cut off for more than one-half of the input signal."

notes.front: What is a linear amplifier?
notes.back: An amplifier in which the output preserves the shape of the input waveform.
notes.explanation: Preserving waveform shape matters for modes like SSB, where the envelope itself carries the audio information.
notes.example: An SSB transmitter's final amplifier must be linear, or the voice waveform becomes distorted.

notes.front: What is amplifier efficiency?
notes.back: The ratio of RF output power to DC input power.
notes.explanation: A higher efficiency means less of the DC power supplied to the amplifier is wasted as heat.
notes.example: A Class C amplifier's high efficiency means comparatively little of its DC input power turns to heat.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 7 glossary: "EFFICIENCY—The ratio of output-signal power compared to the total input power."

notes.front: What does "digital" mean, as applied to a circuit?
notes.back: Working with signals that take only discrete states, usually two, rather than continuously varying values.
notes.explanation: Digital circuits form the basis of computers and other digital equipment, making decisions from those discrete states.
notes.example: A logic gate's output is always either high or low, never some in-between value.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 13: digital logic gates "are the 'decision-making' circuits of computers and other types of digital equipment."

notes.front: What is an AND gate?
notes.back: A logic circuit whose output is high only when both, or all, of its inputs are high at the same time.
notes.explanation: It is one of the basic building blocks of digital logic, used wherever a circuit must check that several conditions are true together.
notes.example: A two-input AND gate whose output goes high only when both input signals are simultaneously true.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 13: "The AND gate is a logic circuit that requires all inputs to be TRUE at the same time in order for the ... output."

notes.front: What is a bit?
notes.back: A single binary digit, the smallest unit of digital information, taking one of two values.
notes.explanation: Digital circuits, including binary counters and shift registers, are built from arrays of circuits that each store or move one bit.
notes.example: A 3-bit binary counter uses three separate flip-flops, each holding one bit.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 13: binary numbers are made of binary digits.

notes.front: What is a binary counter?
notes.back: A digital circuit that counts input pulses and represents the count in binary.
notes.explanation: Each added bit doubles the number of distinct counts the circuit can hold, so an n-bit counter has 2^n possible states.
notes.example: A 3-bit binary counter has 2³ = 8 possible states, counting from 0 through 7.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 9 glossary: "COUNTER—A circuit which counts input pulses."

notes.front: What is a shift register?
notes.back: A clocked array of circuits that passes data in steps along the array, capable of serial-to-parallel and parallel-to-serial conversion.
notes.explanation: Each clock pulse moves every stored bit one position along the register, which is how it converts between serial and parallel data forms.
notes.example: A shift register used to convert an incoming serial data stream into a parallel word for processing.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 13 glossary: "SHIFT REGISTER—A register capable of serial-to-parallel and parallel-to-serial conversion and scaling."

notes.front: What is feedback in an amplifier?
notes.back: The process of sending part of an amplifier's output signal back to its input.
notes.explanation: An oscillator deliberately uses feedback in the right phase to sustain continuous oscillation; unwanted feedback instead causes instability.
notes.example: A sine wave oscillator is built from a filter and an amplifier connected in a feedback loop.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 8 glossary: "FEEDBACK—The process of sending part of an output signal of an amplifier back to the input of the amplifier."

notes.front: What is a tank circuit?
notes.back: A tuned (resonant) circuit used to temporarily store energy, also called a parallel-resonant circuit.
notes.explanation: In an LC oscillator, the tank circuit's inductance and capacitance set the frequency of oscillation.
notes.example: The parallel LC combination at the heart of an LC oscillator is its tank circuit.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 9 glossary: "TANK CIRCUIT—A tuned circuit used to temporarily store energy. Also referred to as a parallel-resonant circuit."

notes.front: What is the purpose of neutralizing an amplifier?
notes.back: To eliminate self-oscillations.
notes.explanation: Neutralization cancels the internal feedback, usually from interelectrode capacitance, that would otherwise sustain unwanted oscillation.

notes.front: Of the four common amplifier classes, which conducts 100% of the time, and which is the most efficient?
notes.back: Class A conducts the full input cycle (100% of the time); Class C is the most efficient.
notes.explanation: Efficiency rises as conduction time falls, so Class C, which conducts for less than half the cycle, wastes the least DC power as heat.
notes.source: NCVEC 2023–2027 General Pool, G7B02, G7B04, G7B11

notes.front: What defines a linear amplifier?
notes.back: The output preserves the shape of the input waveform.
notes.explanation: This makes a linear amplifier essential for SSB, where the transmitted waveform must track the voice signal's varying envelope.

notes.front: How is the efficiency of an RF power amplifier determined?
notes.back: Divide the RF output power by the DC input power.
notes.explanation: This ratio shows how much of the power drawn from the supply is actually converted to useful RF output, rather than lost as heat.

notes.front: How does a two-input AND gate's output depend on its inputs?
notes.back: The output is high only when both inputs are high.
notes.explanation: Any other input combination, including either input low, leaves the AND gate's output low.

notes.front: How many states does a 3-bit binary counter have?
notes.explanation: Each added bit doubles the number of possible states, so three bits give 2 × 2 × 2 = 8.

notes.front: What does a shift register do?
notes.back: It is a clocked array of circuits that passes data in steps along the array.
notes.explanation: Each clock pulse advances every stored bit one place, which is the mechanism behind serial-to-parallel data conversion.

notes.front: What are the basic components of a sine wave oscillator, and what sets an LC oscillator's frequency?
notes.back: A filter and an amplifier operating in a feedback loop; an LC oscillator's frequency is set by the inductance and capacitance in the tank circuit.
notes.explanation: The feedback loop sustains continuous oscillation, while the tank circuit's LC values determine at what frequency that oscillation settles.

notes.front: What is the purpose of neutralizing an amplifier?
notes.back: To eliminate self-oscillations
notes.choices:
A) To limit the modulation index
B) To eliminate self-oscillations
C) To cut off the final amplifier during standby periods
D) To keep the carrier on frequency
notes.choicesExplained: A, C and D describe unrelated amplifier functions; neutralization specifically counteracts the internal feedback that causes self-oscillation.
notes.explanation: Neutralization cancels interelectrode-capacitance feedback that would otherwise make the amplifier oscillate on its own.

notes.front: Which of these classes of amplifiers has the highest efficiency?
notes.back: Class C
notes.choices:
A) Class A
B) Class B
C) Class AB
D) Class C
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and C conduct for a larger portion of the input cycle than Class C, which wastes more DC power as heat and so is less efficient.
notes.explanation: Class C's short conduction period, cut off for more than half the cycle, gives it the least wasted power of the four classes.

notes.front: Which of the following describes the function of a two-input AND gate?
notes.back: Output is high only when both inputs are high
notes.choices:
A) Output is high when either or both inputs are low
B) Output is high only when both inputs are high
C) Output is low when either or both inputs are high
D) Output is low only when both inputs are high
notes.choicesExplained: A and D both describe a gate whose output is high unless both inputs are high, the opposite behaviour to AND. C describes a gate whose output is high only when both inputs are low.
notes.explanation: An AND gate requires all its inputs to be true at the same time to produce a true output.

notes.front: In a Class A amplifier, what percentage of the time does the amplifying device conduct?
notes.choices:
A) 100%
B) More than 50% but less than 100%
C) 50%
D) Less than 50%
notes.choicesExplained: B describes Class AB conduction. C describes Class B. D describes Class C; only Class A conducts for the entire cycle.
notes.explanation: Class A is biased so the device never cuts off, conducting throughout the full input cycle.

notes.front: How many states does a 3-bit binary counter have?
notes.choicesExplained: A confuses the bit count with the number of states. B is not a power of two. D is the state count for four bits, one too many.
notes.explanation: Three bits give 2³ = 8 possible combinations, so the counter has 8 states.

notes.front: What is a shift register?
notes.back: A clocked array of circuits that passes data in steps along the array
notes.choices:
A) A clocked array of circuits that passes data in steps along the array
B) An array of operational amplifiers used for tri-state arithmetic operations
C) A digital mixer
D) An analog mixer
notes.choicesExplained: B describes an invented function that is not what a shift register does. C and D name mixer circuits, unrelated to shifting stored data.
notes.explanation: A shift register moves stored bits one position along the array on each clock pulse.

notes.front: Which of the following are basic components of a sine wave oscillator?
notes.back: A filter and an amplifier operating in a feedback loop
notes.choices:
A) An amplifier and a divider
B) A frequency multiplier and a mixer
C) A circulator and a filter operating in a feed-forward loop
D) A filter and an amplifier operating in a feedback loop
notes.choicesExplained: A and B name circuits that do not by themselves sustain oscillation. C names the wrong loop type; oscillation needs feedback, not feed-forward.
notes.explanation: The feedback loop sustains continuous oscillation, while the filter shapes which frequency is reinforced.

notes.front: How is the efficiency of an RF power amplifier determined?
notes.back: Divide the RF output power by the DC input power
notes.choices:
A) Divide the DC input power by the DC output power
B) Divide the RF output power by the DC input power
C) Multiply the RF input power by the reciprocal of the RF output power
D) Add the RF input power to the DC output power
notes.choicesExplained: A divides the wrong pair of quantities. C and D describe operations that do not produce an efficiency ratio at all.
notes.explanation: Efficiency compares useful RF output power against the DC power drawn to produce it.

notes.front: What determines the frequency of an LC oscillator?
notes.back: The inductance and capacitance in the tank circuit
notes.choices:
A) The number of stages in the counter
B) The number of stages in the divider
C) The inductance and capacitance in the tank circuit
D) The time delay of the lag circuit
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and D describe circuits that could set a digital or resistor-capacitor timing, but they are not what sets an LC oscillator's resonant frequency.
notes.explanation: An LC oscillator's frequency is the resonant frequency of its tank circuit, set by that inductance and capacitance.

notes.front: Which of the following describes a linear amplifier?
notes.back: An amplifier in which the output preserves the input waveform
notes.choices:
A) Any RF power amplifier used in conjunction with an amateur transceiver
B) An amplifier in which the output preserves the input waveform
C) A Class C high efficiency amplifier
D) An amplifier used as a frequency multiplier
notes.choicesExplained: A is too broad; not every RF power amplifier used with a transceiver is linear. C describes a highly non-linear amplifier type. D describes a different function entirely.
notes.explanation: Preserving the input waveform shape, not any other property, is what defines a linear amplifier.

notes.front: For which of the following modes is a Class C power stage appropriate for amplifying a modulated signal?
notes.back: FM
notes.choices:
A) SSB
B) FM
C) AM
D) All these choices are correct
notes.choicesExplained: A and C carry information in their amplitude envelope, which a non-linear Class C stage would distort; D is wrong because A and C are not suitable.
notes.explanation: FM carries its information in frequency, not amplitude, so a Class C stage's amplitude distortion does no harm.

notes.front: How do Class A and Class C amplifiers compare in conduction time and efficiency?
notes.back: Class A conducts the full cycle: low distortion, low efficiency. Class C conducts under half the cycle: high distortion, the best efficiency.
notes.explanation: Shorter conduction time saves DC power but badly distorts the waveform, which is why the choice depends on the mode being amplified.

notes.front: Why does SSB need a linear amplifier while FM can use an efficient Class C stage?
notes.back: SSB carries information in its amplitude envelope, so it needs a linear stage; FM carries information only in frequency, so amplitude distortion does not matter.
notes.explanation: Confusing which mode tolerates non-linear amplification is a common way to get an amplifier-class question wrong.
